title: Hepatic-metastasized adenocarcinomas of the stomach and gastroesophageal junction: multimodal treatment with gastrectomy/esophagectomy and resection or ablation of the metastases
summary:
Cancers of the stomach and esophagus are among the most common types of cancer worldwide. Unfortunately, many patients already have secondary tumors (so-called metastases) in other organs at the time of their first diagnosis. In such cases, the disease is usually no longer curable, and treatment is limited to what is known as palliative chemotherapy, meaning a treatment aimed at slowing the progression of the disease and alleviating symptoms.
An operation that removes both the original tumor and the metastases is generally not performed in this situation. However, in other types of cancer (such as colorectal cancer) such an operation, when performed in addition to palliative chemotherapy, has been shown in certain cases to prolong survival.
Previous studies on stomach and esophageal cancer that investigated such operations have produced mixed results. Some studies were unable to show a clear benefit, partly because many patients were no longer fit enough to receive further chemotherapy after surgery, or because complications occurred more frequently.
In this study, we aim to investigate whether a combination of (immuno-)chemotherapy and modern, minimally invasive surgical techniques can improve treatment outcomes, particularly by prolonging overall survival while maintaining quality of life.
The tumor in the stomach or esophagus is to be removed. Existing metastases are also to be surgically removed or treated using modern procedures (e.g., local ablation).
An important difference from earlier studies is the use of minimally invasive, robot-assisted surgical techniques. These procedures are generally gentler, cause less pain, and allow faster recovery. The goal is that more patients—if recommended by a tumor board—can better tolerate chemotherapy after surgery, which in turn may improve their chances of longer survival.
In addition, modern treatment combinations are made possible, in which traditional chemotherapy is combined with new immunotherapies and antibody therapies. Thus, in this study, surgical removal of the tumors along with all metastases can be offered as an additional therapeutic option to the most advanced systemic treatments.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Histologically confirmed gastric or gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma with hepatic metastases
Medical and technical resectability of the primary tumor: metastatic lesions are resectable or can be controlled by a local ablative procedure (interdisciplinary assessment)
Existing recommendation from an interdisciplinary tumor board supporting resection as part of an individualized treatment concept
Additional non-hepatic metastases may be included: Localized, potentially resectable peritoneal carcinomatosis; Lung: potentially resectable or otherwise treatable; unilateral or bilateral Krukenberg tumors (ovarian metastases); Unilateral or bilateral adrenal metastases; Extra-abdominal lymph node metastases such as supraclavicular or cervical lymph node involvement; Localized bone involvement (defined as within a radiation field) or other metastatic disease sites deemed resectable by the investigator and confirmed by the review committee
The patient is mentally and physically capable of understanding the meaning and implications of the study
Written informed consent
Exclusion criteria:
Functional inoperability
Non-resectable primary tumor (adenocarcinoma of the stomach or gastroesophageal junction)
Concurrent participation in another interventional study
Pregnancy
Severe psychopathological findings and pre-existing conditions, e.g., active psychosis
